summary: Defines requirements for DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) protocols that enable coordinated response to distributed denial-of-service attacks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of what an alarm system must do so a victim can quickly ask others for help when flooded with traffic.

subtitle: What a standard protocol for asking other networks for help during a DDoS attack must be able to do.

tldr.problem: DDoS mitigation services each offer proprietary interfaces, which tie a subscriber to one service and leave operators in the attack path unable to help, so responses can be fragmented or incomplete.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets requirements for DOTS: a small, resilient signal channel for mitigation requests and status, a reliable data channel for bulk configuration, strong security, and a data model.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document that guides the DOTS protocol designs. It does not define a protocol or how mitigation itself is carried out.

facts.label: Required scope types
facts.value: IPv4 prefixes, IPv6 prefixes, domain names

today: RFC 8612 is an Informational document and the data lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements for DOTS protocols and data models rather than defining a protocol itself.

sections.title: Why DOTS Is Needed
sections.content:
Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks are common, and high-volume attacks that saturate inbound links are now frequent. Many enterprises cannot run mitigation themselves, so service providers offer on-demand traffic scrubbing, which separates attack traffic from legitimate traffic and forwards only the latter.

Today these services use proprietary interfaces. A standard way to coordinate a real-time response among operators should speed up and strengthen mitigation. DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) communicates the need for defensive action before or during an attack, but it does not dictate how that action is carried out. This RFC describes the required characteristics of such protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now every helper has its own private phone number and rules. One shared emergency number would let everyone cooperate faster.

sections.title: The Cast of DOTS Agents
sections.content:
A DOTS client asks for attack response. A DOTS server handles those requests, passes them to a mitigator (the entity that actually performs mitigation) and returns selected feedback. A DOTS gateway joins a server and a client into one agent, like a SIP Back-to-Back User Agent, so it can sit between downstream clients and upstream servers. DOTS agent covers all of these.

The signal channel is a bidirectional, mutually authenticated channel that stays resilient under severe packet loss. The data channel is used for infrequent but reliable bulk exchange and is not expected to work during congestion. A drop-list names sources to block regardless of content, and an accept-list names sources always to allow.
sections.plainLanguage: A client is the one shouting for help, a server is the one who answers, and the mitigator is the one who actually pushes the bad traffic away.

sections.title: General Requirements
sections.content:
Requirements are named with IDs such as GEN-001 and use the RFC 2119 keywords. The general ones are:

  • Extensibility (GEN-001): protocols and data models MUST be extensible and backward compatible. Older implementations MUST ignore optional information from newer versions and MUST reject mandatory information they do not understand.
  • Resilience (GEN-002): the signaling protocol MUST maximize the chance of delivery under attack conditions and keep working despite message loss and out-of-order or redundant delivery.
  • Bulk data (GEN-003): a separate, secure data channel with reliable transport MUST be used for bulk exchange.
  • Mitigation hinting (GEN-004): clients MAY send hints over the signal channel, and servers MAY ignore them.
  • Loop handling (GEN-005): implementations should be ready to detect and end loops caused by misconfigured DNS or routing.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must be able to grow, keep working even when messages get lost, and have a second slower line for big packages of information.

sections.title: The Signal Channel
sections.content:
The signal channel has the most requirements (SIG-001 to SIG-011). It SHOULD use connectionless transport such as UDP, with TCP MAY be used if network policy requires. Messages MUST stay under the path MTU, assuming 1280 bytes if it cannot be discovered, or optionally 576 bytes for IPv4. The channel MUST be bidirectional, and agents MUST exchange heartbeats, which keep NAT and firewall bindings alive. During active mitigation the channel should not be torn down just because heartbeats are lost, since loss is likely in a volumetric attack.

Authorized clients MUST be able to request scoped mitigation and servers MUST send status, including a reason when a request is rejected, and metrics for packets and bytes blocked (total and per second). Clients can withdraw a request at any time. A server MAY keep mitigating for a limited active-but-terminating period, up to a maximum of 300 seconds (5 minutes), to absorb flapping. Every request MUST include a lifetime, and servers MUST support renewing it.

Scope MUST support IPv4 prefixes, IPv6 prefixes and domain names, with URIs optional, plus scope aliases. Servers in one domain SHALL detect conflicting requests and notify the clients. A signal channel using UDP MUST include a congestion control mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The emergency line uses tiny messages so they get through a traffic jam. Both sides keep saying hello to show they are still there, and each help request says what to protect and for how long.

sections.title: The Data Channel and Data Model
sections.content:
The data channel handles configuration and management and is not built for attack conditions. Messages MUST be delivered reliably and in order (DATA-001). Servers MUST provide an interface to configure resource identifiers such as scope aliases, and MUST let clients manage drop-lists and accept-lists by creating, retrieving, updating and deleting entries.

The data model requirements (DM-001 to DM-009) say it MUST be versioned and able to represent mitigation requests and withdrawal, status including failures and their causes, extensible scope, lifetime including no end time, perceived efficacy, preferred heartbeat interval, and acceptable signal loss. It MUST NOT bake in assumptions about a particular transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides the quick emergency line there is a slower, reliable mailbox for long lists, like which visitors are always welcome and which are banned.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Risks
sections.content:
DOTS must be strict about security, since a weak channel could enable the very attacks it should stop. Agents MUST authenticate each other (SEC-001), protect confidentiality, integrity and authenticity with TLS or DTLS and current IETF best practices (RFC 7525), detect replayed messages (SEC-004), and have servers authorize all client messages about mitigation, configuration, filtering or status (SEC-005).

The RFC says the document has no security considerations of its own, but warns about impersonation and signal blocking. An attacker impersonating a client could install drop-lists blocking all inbound traffic to networks the client may protect. An impersonated server could act as a malicious gateway and discard mitigation requests. Operators should monitor and audit DOTS agents. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster could pretend to be the caller, they might get the helpers to block everyone. So both sides must prove who they are and keep messages secret and fresh.
